summary.text: A large igneous province is a huge build-up of igneous rock, both underground sills and dikes and surface lava flows, formed as magma travels up through the crust.
When formed they often cover a few million square kilometres with around a million cubic kilometres of rock, and most of a basaltic one is usually laid down in under a million years.
Some formed at the same time as mass extinctions and rapid climate change, and some of those changes came from fast releases of greenhouse gases.

facts.label: Linked metals
facts.value: Copper–nickel, iron, platinum group, titanium, vanadium

items.prompt: Rocks from a single ancient lava province now turn up in Brazil, eastern North America and northwest Africa. How did they end up so far apart?

options.label: Three separate eruptions happened at once
Lava flowed across the Atlantic seafloor
Plate movements split the province apart
Ocean currents scattered the cooled rock

items.explain: Some provinces, like the Central Atlantic magmatic province, have been fragmented and separated by plate movements.

items.prompt: Why might people studying today's climate look closely at lava floods from hundreds of millions of years ago?

options.label: They quickly released greenhouse gases, much like today
Their rocks absorb carbon dioxide from the air now
They show that climate never changes very fast
Their eruptions are still warming the planet today

items.explain: Some past changes came from rapid releases of greenhouse gases, so these events can serve as cases for understanding current and future change.

items.prompt: What is one of the big puzzles about how these provinces form?

options.label: Why their rock is never found on land
How so much magma erupted so quickly
Why they appear only in the oceans
How they formed without any heat

items.explain: Enormous volumes of basalt were made and erupted over short time scales, at rates up to ten times those of mid-ocean ridges.

items.prompt: A geologist maps a wide area of basalt seafloor made at an ordinary mid-ocean ridge. Does it count as a large igneous province?

options.label: Yes, any wide area of basalt qualifies
Yes, if it formed in under a million years
Only if fossils are found buried inside it
No, normal plate-tectonic seafloor is left out

items.explain: Basalt sea floors and other products of normal plate tectonics were not included in the definition.

items.prompt: Why do mining companies take an interest in these provinces?

options.label: Their basalt is soft and cheap to quarry
They hold thick beds of rock salt and potash
They are linked to nickel, copper and platinum ores
They contain most of the world's coal seams

items.explain: They are associated with copper–nickel and iron concentrations and platinum group element deposits.

items.prompt: Hot mantle rising in a plume spreads out beneath a tectonic plate. What can that do at the surface?

options.label: Push the region upward
Pull the region downward
Freeze the plate in place
Flood the region with sea

items.explain: Plume material spreading radially under a plate causes regions of uplift, and such plumes play an important role in forming these provinces.
